models.approach: Show that the status gap is manufactured by funding and selection, then argue for parity on labour-market grounds.
plan: Introduction: the disagreement, and where you land.
Body 1: the case for university priority, put fairly.
Body 2: the case for parity, with the shortage evidence.
Conclusion: your opinion, and what parity would require.

paras.text: [[It is often argued]] that vocational training deserves equal standing with a degree, and equally that universities must remain the priority. Having weighed both, [[I would maintain]] that parity is the better policy, and that the present hierarchy is largely an artefact of how the two are funded.

[[On the one hand]], the defence of university priority is not empty. Research capacity resides there, and a country that neglects it loses the [[intellectual]] base on which its industries eventually depend. [[It is true that]] graduates still earn more on average and that broad academic study develops judgement that a narrow qualification does not, which is why parents push their children towards it.

[[On the other hand]], the shortages are almost entirely technical. Electricians, welders, technicians and care workers are scarce across Europe while graduate underemployment rises, so the signal from the labour market is [[explicit]] and has been ignored for a generation. [[There is evidence that]] a skilled trade in Germany or Switzerland, where apprenticeships are funded and respected, pays comparably to many degrees, which shows the status gap is a policy outcome rather than a natural ranking. [[Consequently]], the [[dearth]] of technicians is manufactured by the funding, not by the young.

[[All things considered]], my own view is that the two routes should carry equal funding, equal maintenance support and equal standing in the school system. That means paying for apprenticeships properly and, [[importantly]], allowing movement between the routes, since a hierarchy is [[ingrained]] most deeply when the ladder only runs one way.

notes: Naming the German and Swiss comparison converts a claim about status into an argument about policy.
The observation that shortages are technical while graduate underemployment rises is the evidence the position rests on.
The movement between routes condition is the detail that makes parity meaningful rather than declared.

models.approach: Defend the broader education while conceding that vocational funding is inadequate.
plan: Introduction: the disagreement, and which side you finish on.
Body 1: the parity case, fully stated.
Body 2: what a university does that training does not.
Conclusion: your opinion, with the concession built in.

paras.text: [[It is arguable whether]] vocational training and degrees should carry equal weight, and the answer depends on what education is being asked to do. [[In my opinion]] universities should remain the priority, though the underfunding of vocational routes is a genuine scandal.

[[On the one hand]], the case for parity is strong on immediate need. Shortages of technicians are acute, apprenticeships lead to secure work, and the assumption that everybody should take a degree has left many graduates with debt and a job that never required one. [[It must be acknowledged]] that the contempt directed at technical education is snobbery rather than analysis.

[[On the other hand]], the two are not substitutes. A vocational qualification trains for a known occupation, and its value depends on that occupation continuing to exist, which is precisely what automation makes uncertain. A broad education develops the capacity to learn something else, which is [[intrinsic]] to a working life that will now contain several changes of trade. [[It is worth noting]] that universities also carry research, and a country that treats them as one training route among many will find the research capacity [[irrecoverable]] once it has gone.

[[On balance]], I would keep universities as the priority and fund vocational training far better than at present, which is not a contradiction: the argument is about the ranking of purposes rather than of people. [[In essence]] the state should pay for what the market will not, and the market underprovides both basic research and the apprenticeship it cannot recoup, which makes the [[dichotomy]] a false one.

notes: Conceding that the contempt for technical education is snobbery removes the worst reading of this position before it is made.
The argument that vocational value depends on the occupation surviving is the strongest available defence of broad education.
The final sentence dissolves the opposition rather than winning it, which is a mature finish.

models.stance: The question conflates funding with status
models.approach: Argue that funding parity is straightforward and status parity is a separate, harder problem.
plan: Introduction: two claims are bundled; separate them.
Body 1: funding, where parity is straightforwardly right.
Body 2: status, which policy cannot simply legislate.
Conclusion: your opinion on each, and what would move the second.

paras.text: The debate bundles two claims: that vocational training should be funded equally and that it should be regarded equally. [[From my perspective]] the first is straightforwardly right and the second cannot be delivered by funding alone, which is why decades of announcements have changed so little.

[[On the one hand]], the funding case is close to unanswerable. A country short of electricians and long on unemployed graduates is misallocating its education budget, and apprenticeships return their cost quickly through wages and taxes. [[There is evidence that]] every serious economy with a strong technical sector funds it publicly rather than leaving it to employers, who will not pay to train somebody a competitor may hire. [[Consequently]], funding parity is a [[pragmatic]] measure rather than an act of generosity.

[[On the other hand]], status follows the choices of the people making them, not the intentions of ministers. Parents steer children towards degrees because a degree remains the safer signal to employers, and that will persist while the professions recruit almost exclusively from graduates. [[It must be acknowledged]] that governments have declared parity repeatedly and the [[propensity]] to choose university has barely moved. [[More precisely]], status will change when employers open senior routes to technical qualifications, which is a slower and less [[intelligible|Intelligible]] lever.

[[Taken together]], I support funding parity immediately and regard status parity as a longer project that requires employers rather than education ministries. [[In essence]] the two sides of this debate are arguing about different timescales, and separating them would produce agreement on the half that can be acted on now.

notes: Separating funding from status explains why the debate never resolves, and it lets the essay agree with both camps precisely.
The observation that employers, not ministries, control status is the essay's most useful claim.
Different timescales is a diagnosis of the disagreement itself, which is a strong way to close.
